1.p: Why should you keep away from the rock walls at this geosite?
r: Cracks separate blocks (“wedges”) that can slide and fall
The rock is still hot from volcanic activity
1.e: Fractures with different orientations isolate unstable blocks called wedges. Pulled by gravity, they can slide and fall to the side of the road.

2.p: What is the dike you can see at this geosite?
r: An intrusive rock: magma that cooled inside a fracture of an older rock
A lava flow that ran over the surface
A wall built to hold back water on the hill
2.e: About 21 million years ago, magma entered a fracture in older volcanic rocks and cooled there, forming a slab-shaped body: a dike. That is why the dike is younger than the rock that contains it.

3.p: What is the name of the transformation of rocks at the surface, by physical disintegration and chemical decomposition, that gives rise to soil?
3.e: Weathering happens in place: temperature, humidity, water and living things break down and decompose the rock. Erosion, by contrast, wears material away and carries it off. Weathered rock plus organic matter forms soil.

4.p: How can you recognize the pyroxene crystals in this intrusive rock?
r: They are dark and more or less rectangular, up to several centimeters long
They are transparent like glass and rounded
They are white and form thin layers
4.e: Pyroxenes stand out because of their dark color and more or less rectangular shapes. In the images they are painted green to highlight them.

5.p: What do the sheets produced by spheroidal weathering look like?
5.e: Water attacks the blocks from their edges and creates concentric sheets, like the layers of an onion, around a sounder, rounded core of rock.

6.p: Roughly how old are the volcanic and intrusive rocks that meet here?
6.e: The oldest volcanic rocks of San Cristóbal Hill are about 28 million years old; the intrusive rocks that cut through them are about 21 million years old.

7.p: What are the flattened volcanic fragments in a welded tuff called?
7.e: They are fragments of pumice or volcanic glass that landed while still hot and soft; the weight of the layers above flattened and welded them into lens-like shapes. Because of their shape they are called fiamme (“flames” in Italian).

8.p: What kind of rock is the rock in the Tupahue pool?
r: A welded tuff: volcanic fragments that landed while still hot and welded together
A block of granite brought from the Andes
A sedimentary rock formed at the bottom of a lake
8.e: It is a welded tuff, like the one at Geosite 7: during an explosive eruption the rock fragments thrown out landed while still hot and were flattened and welded together. The rock lay at the bottom of the old quarry, and the architect decided to make it part of the pool.

Cordón Cerro San Cristóbal.desc: The volcanic rocks we see from San Cristóbal Hill to the La Pirámide area formed during successive very violent volcanic eruptions, with huge explosions that threw out gases, ash and glowing rock fragments.

Cerro El Carbón 1.desc: The volcanic rocks of this unit formed during successive very violent volcanic eruptions, with huge explosions that threw out gases, ash and glowing rock fragments.

Cerro Blanco.desc: The rocks of Cerro Blanco formed during successive very violent volcanic eruptions, with huge explosions that threw out gases, ash and glowing rock fragments.

Cerro El Carbón 2.desc: The volcanic rocks of this unit formed during successive volcanic eruptions dominated by lava flowing from a vent that may have been located a little to the north and east of Cerro El Carbón.

Pórfido andesítico.desc: The rocks of this unit formed at depth when magma cooled in the feeder conduits of volcanoes or their magma chambers, about 21 million years ago.
